explain.say: If a lion catches one zebra, an animal in a group of a hundred has a far smaller chance of being that one than an animal alone. This is the dilution effect, and the animals in the middle of the group are safest of all.

A herd running together is also confusing: a predator finds it hard to fix on one animal among many moving bodies. But herds have costs too, such as competing for food and spreading disease more easily.

faq.q: How does a herd spot predators?
faq.a: Every animal in the herd is watching, listening and smelling, so a predator is usually noticed sooner. When one animal startles or calls, the alarm spreads through the whole group.
asks: Why are herds good at spotting lions?
How do herd animals warn each other?

faq.a: The dilution effect means that the bigger the group, the smaller each animal's chance of being the one a predator catches. With a hundred zebras, the risk is shared a hundred ways.
asks: What does safety in numbers mean?

faq.q: Why are animals in the middle of a herd safest?
faq.a: Predators usually attack from the edge, so animals at the centre are surrounded by others. Biologist W. D. Hamilton called this the selfish herd: each animal tries to put others between itself and danger.
asks: Why do animals crowd together when attacked?

faq.a: Stripes might make it harder to pick out one zebra in a running herd, but the strongest evidence is that they put off biting flies, which find it hard to land on striped surfaces.

faq.q: Are there downsides to living in a herd?
faq.a: Yes. Animals in a herd compete for food and water, diseases and parasites spread more easily, and a big herd is easy for predators to find.
asks: What are the problems with living in groups?
Why don't all animals live in herds?

facts: W. D. Hamilton described the selfish herd in 1971, explaining why animals crowd towards the centre of a group.
Experiments suggest zebra stripes strongly deter biting flies from landing (Caro and colleagues, 2019).
